content: Dental fillings, also known as dental restorations, are materials used to artificially restore the function, integrity, and morphology of missing tooth structure. This structural loss typically occurs due to dental caries (tooth decay) or external trauma. In some cases, tooth structure is intentionally removed during preparation to enhance the aesthetics or physical integrity of the restorative material. Dental restorations can also involve replacing missing tooth structure with dental implants. Dental restorations are made from a variety of materials. Common direct restorative materials include dental amalgam, glass ionomer cement, and composite resins. Indirect restorative materials often include acrylic, porcelain, zirconia, gold, and other metals. Restorations are broadly categorized into direct and indirect types, and they can be further classified based on their location and size. If decay extends beyond the dentin, root canal therapy is performed, followed by the placement of a crown. Tooth Preparation Tooth preparation involves removing infected or decayed tooth material to clean and shape the cavity for filling. This is typically done using a dental drill. If a permanent restoration cannot be placed immediately after preparation, a temporary restoration is used. Direct Restorations Direct restorations are applied directly to the tooth in situ. Materials such as dental amalgam (silver-colored) or composite resin (tooth-colored) are commonly used. When composite resin is used, the filling is cured using a blue-spectrum light (not UV light) and may also be polished. Patients are advised to avoid chewing hard foods for a day or two after the procedure to prevent dislodging the filling. Indirect Restorations Indirect restorations include inlays, onlays, crowns, bridges, and veneers. These are fabricated outside the mouth, typically in a dental laboratory, based on impressions or digital scans of the prepared tooth. Once the fit and bite are confirmed, the restoration is permanently bonded to the tooth. While waiting for the indirect restoration to be completed, a temporary restoration may be placed to protect the prepared tooth, maintain occlusal space, and preserve periodontal health. Removable dental prostheses, such as dentures, are sometimes considered a form of indirect restoration. Precision attachments like magnets, clips, hooks, or implants may be used to secure removable prosthetics. Restoration with Dental Implants Dental implants are increasingly used in restorative dentistry due to advancements in technology and research. Implants, typically made of titanium or titanium alloy, are screws anchored into the maxillary or mandibular bone. They are used to support crowns, bridges, or prostheses. Ideally, the bone integrates with the implant's roughened surface, a process known as osseointegration. Restoration Classifications G.V. Black classified restorations based on their size and location. For instance, a one-surface filling is categorized as Class I under Black's system. Materials Used in Dental Restorations Metals and Metallic Alloys: These are commonly used for crowns, bridges, and dentures. Pure titanium is biocompatible and integrates well with bone. Other materials include high-gold-content alloys, gold-platinum alloys, and silver-palladium alloys. Base Metallic Alloys: Examples include cobalt-chromium and nickel-chromium alloys. Amalgam: A traditional material used for direct fillings. Dental Composites Dental composites, also known as white fillings, are resin-based materials used in direct fillings. They consist of a resin matrix (e.g., bisphenol A-glycidyl methacrylate or urethane dimethacrylate) and an inorganic filler (e.g., silica). The filler provides wear resistance and translucency, while a coupling agent like silane enhances the bond between the resin and filler. An initiator package triggers polymerization when external energy (light or heat) is applied. Composites are also used for inlays, onlays, crowns, and veneers. While aesthetically pleasing, they are less durable than porcelain or metal restorations and are prone to wear and discoloration. Glass Ionomer Cement (GIC) Glass ionomer cement is a tooth-colored material introduced in 1972 for use in anterior teeth restorations, particularly in eroded areas and Class III and V cavities. It chemically bonds to dental hard tissues and releases fluoride over time, making it suitable for low-stress areas like smooth surfaces and small anterior proximal cavities in primary teeth. However, clinical studies do not support its use in primary molars. Porcelain and Ceramic Restorations Porcelain restorations, such as veneers and full-ceramic crowns, are highly desirable due to their natural tooth-like color and translucency. Porcelain-fused-to-metal restorations combine the strength of metal with the aesthetics of porcelain, making them durable and resistant to wear. The advent of CAD/CAM technology has enabled the use of zirconium oxide (ZrO2) in restorative and prosthetic dentistry. Zirconium oxide is strong, fracture-resistant, and suitable for full-ceramic prosthetic solutions, including bridges and implant structures. Its application was previously limited due to processing challenges, but computerized dentistry has made its use more practical and economical. CAD/CAM Dental Restorations The CEREC method is a chairside CAD/CAM restorative procedure. The dentist examines the tooth and determines the appropriate treatment, which could range from a simple filling to a full crown, depending on the remaining healthy tooth structure. An optical impression of the prepared tooth is taken using a camera, and specialized software converts the image into a 3D virtual model. The restoration design data is sent to a milling machine, which fabricates an all-ceramic, tooth-colored restoration in about 10–20 minutes. The restoration is then bonded in place.
